blocks.p: As I walked through the wilderness of this world, I came to a certain place where there was a den, and I lay down there to sleep; and as I slept, I dreamed a dream.

I dreamed, and I saw a man dressed in rags, standing in a field with his back to his own house, a book in his hand and a great burden on his back. [Isa. 64:6; Luke 14:33; Ps. 38:4; Hab. 2:2; Acts 16:30-31] I watched him open the book and read, and as he read he wept and trembled, until he could hold it in no longer and broke out in an anguished cry: “What shall I do?” [Acts 2:37]

In this state he went home and held himself together as long as he could, so that his wife and children would not see his distress. But he could not stay silent for long, because his trouble kept growing. At last he opened his mind to them.

“My dear wife,” he said, “and you, my children, my own flesh and blood: I, your dear friend, am undone. A burden lies on me that I cannot carry. Worse than that, I have it on good authority that this city of ours will be burned with fire from heaven, and in that terrible overthrow all of us, I and you my wife and you my sweet children, will come to a miserable end, unless some way of escape can be found. And I do not yet see one.”

His family was stunned, not because they believed a word of it, but because they thought some fever had got into his head. Since night was coming on, and they hoped sleep might settle his brain, they hurried him off to bed. But the night was as bad as the day. Instead of sleeping, he spent it in sighs and tears. In the morning they asked how he was.
“Worse and worse,” he said, and began talking to them again.

Now they started to harden against him. They tried to drive out his sickness with harshness, sometimes mocking him, sometimes scolding him, sometimes ignoring him altogether. So he took to shutting himself in his room, where he prayed for them and pitied them and grieved over his own misery. He would also walk alone in the fields, sometimes reading, sometimes praying. And so he spent his days.

Then I saw, one day while he was walking in the fields, that he was reading in his book as usual and in great distress of mind. As he read, he burst out as he had before: “What shall I do to be saved?”

I saw him look this way and that, as if he wanted to run; yet he stood still, because, as far as I could tell, he did not know which way to go. Then I saw a man named Evangelist coming toward him. [Job 33:23]
“Why are you crying out?” Evangelist asked.

“Sir,” the man answered, “I see by this book in my hand that I am condemned to die, and after that to face judgment [Heb. 9:27]; and I find that I am not willing to do the first [Job 16:21], and not able to do the second.” [Ezek. 22:14]

v: No sooner has Christian left the world than he
is met by Evangelist, who lovingly
brings news of another world, and shows the way
to climb to it from where he stands today.

blocks.p: “Why not willing to die,” said Evangelist, “when this life is full of so many evils?”

“Because I’m afraid that this burden on my back will sink me lower than the grave, and I will fall into Tophet. [Isa. 30:33] And sir, if I’m not fit to go to prison, I am certainly not fit to go to judgment, and from there to execution. The thought of these things is what makes me cry out.”
“If that is your condition,” said Evangelist, “why are you standing still?”
“Because I don’t know where to go.”
Then Evangelist gave him a parchment scroll, and written on it were the words: Flee from the wrath to come. [Matt. 3:7]
The man read it, and looking at Evangelist very carefully, he said, “Where must I flee to?”
Evangelist pointed across a very wide field. “Do you see that narrow gate over there, the Wicket Gate?” [Matt. 7:13-14]
“No,” said the man.
“Do you see that shining light?” [Ps. 119:105; 2 Pet. 1:19]
“I think I do.”
“Keep that light in your eye,” said Evangelist, “and go straight toward it. Then you will see the gate. Knock there, and you will be told what to do.”
So I saw in my dream that the man began to run.

He had not run far from his own door when his wife and children saw him and began to cry out after him to come back. But the man put his fingers in his ears and ran on, crying, “Life! Life! Eternal life!” [Luke 14:26] He did not look behind him, but fled toward the middle of the plain. [Gen. 19:17]

The neighbors came out to watch him run. [Jer. 20:10] Some mocked, some threatened, and some called after him to turn back. Among these were two who decided to fetch him back by force. One was named Obstinate, and the other Pliable. By now the man had a good lead on them, but they were determined, and before long they caught up with him.
“Neighbors,” said the man, “why have you come?”
“To persuade you to come back with us.”

“That’s impossible,” he said. “You live in the City of Destruction, the place where I was born. I see it now for what it is. If you die there, sooner or later you will sink lower than the grave, into a place that burns with fire and brimstone. Be reasonable, good neighbors, and come along with me.”
“What!” said Obstinate. “And leave our friends and our comforts behind?”

“Yes,” said Christian, for that was his name, “because everything you would give up is not worth comparing with a little of what I am going to find. [2 Cor. 4:18] And if you come with me and hold on, you’ll do as well as I do; for where I’m going there is enough and to spare. [Luke 15:17] Come on, and prove me right.”
“What is it you’re looking for, that you’d leave the whole world to find it?”

“I’m looking for an inheritance that cannot perish, spoil, or fade [1 Pet. 1:4], laid up safely in heaven [Heb. 11:16], to be given at the appointed time to those who seek it with all their heart. Read it for yourself, if you like. It’s here in my book.”
“Nonsense!” said Obstinate. “Away with your book. Are you coming back with us or not?”
“No, not I,” said Christian. “I have put my hand to the plow.” [Luke 9:62]

“Come on then, neighbor Pliable, let’s turn around and go home without him. There’s a whole breed of these crack-brained fools who, once they get an idea in their heads, think themselves wiser than seven men who can give a reason.” [Prov. 26:16]
“Don’t insult him,” said Pliable. “If what good Christian says is true, the things he’s after are better than ours. My heart is inclined to go with my neighbor.”
“What, another fool? Listen to me and go back. Who knows where a lunatic like this will lead you? Go back, go back, and be sensible.”

“No, come with your neighbor, Pliable,” said Christian. “What I’ve told you is real, and there’s far more glory besides. If you don’t believe me, read it here in this book; and as for the truth of what’s written in it, all of it is sealed with the blood of the One who made it.” [Heb. 9:17-22; 13:20]

“Well, neighbor Obstinate,” said Pliable, “I’m coming to a decision. I intend to go along with this good man and throw in my lot with him.” Then he turned to Christian. “But, my good companion, do you know the way to this place we both want?”
“I’ve been directed by a man named Evangelist to hurry to a little gate ahead of us, where we’ll receive instructions about the way.”
“Come on then, good neighbor, let’s be going.” And the two of them went on together.
“And I will go back home,” said Obstinate. “I’ll be no companion to such deluded, fantastical fellows.”
Now I saw in my dream that when Obstinate had gone back, Christian and Pliable walked on across the plain, talking as they went.

“Well, neighbor Pliable,” said Christian, “how are you? I’m glad you were persuaded to come with me. If even Obstinate had felt what I’ve felt of the power and terror of the unseen world, he wouldn’t have turned his back on us so lightly.”
“Come, neighbor Christian, since there’s no one here but the two of us, tell me more about these things: what they are, and how they’re enjoyed, where we’re going.”
“I can picture them better in my mind than describe them with my tongue. These are things of God, beyond words. But since you want to know, I’ll read about them from my book.”
“And do you think the words of your book are really true?”
“Yes, certainly. It was written by One who cannot lie.” [Titus 1:2]
“Good. What things are they, then?”
“There is an endless kingdom to live in, and everlasting life to be given us, so that we can live in that kingdom forever.” [Isa. 45:17; John 10:28-29]
“Good. And what else?”
“There are crowns of glory to be given us, and robes that will make us shine like the sun in the sky.” [2 Tim. 4:8; Rev. 3:4; Matt. 13:43]
“That’s very pleasant. And what else?”
“There will be no more crying, and no more sorrow, for the Owner of the place will wipe every tear from our eyes.” [Isa. 25:6-8; Rev. 7:17; 21:4]
“And what company will we have there?”

“There we will be with seraphim and cherubim, creatures so bright your eyes will barely stand to look at them. [Isa. 6:2] There you’ll meet thousands upon thousands who have gone before us to that place, none of them harmful, all of them loving and holy, every one walking in the sight of God and standing in his presence, accepted, forever. [1 Thess. 4:16-17; Rev. 5:11] In short: there we’ll see the elders with their golden crowns [Rev. 4:4]; there we’ll see the holy virgins with their golden harps [Rev. 14:1-5]; there we’ll see men who in this world were cut to pieces, burned alive, eaten by beasts, drowned in the sea, for the love they had for the Lord of the place, all of them well, and clothed with immortality like a garment.” [John 12:25; 2 Cor. 5:4]
“Just hearing this is enough to carry a heart away. But can these things really be ours? How do we get our share?”
“The Lord, the Governor of that country, has recorded it in this book. The substance of it is this: if we are truly willing to have it, he will give it to us freely.”
“Well, my good companion, I’m glad to hear it. Come on, let’s pick up the pace.”
“I can’t go as fast as I’d like,” said Christian, “because of this burden on my back.”

Now I saw in my dream that just as they finished this conversation, they came to a very muddy swamp in the middle of the plain; and not paying attention, they both fell suddenly into the bog. The name of the swamp was Despair. Here they wallowed for a time, badly smeared with mud; and Christian, because of the burden on his back, began to sink.
“Ah, neighbor Christian,” said Pliable, “where are we now?”
“Honestly,” said Christian, “I don’t know.”

At this Pliable took offense, and said angrily, “Is this the happiness you’ve been telling me about all this time? If we have this kind of luck at our very first step, what can we expect between here and the end of the journey? If I get out of this alive, you can have your wonderful country to yourself.” And with a desperate struggle or two he got out of the mud on the side of the swamp nearest his own house, and off he went; and Christian never saw him again.

So Christian was left to flounder in the Swamp of Despair alone. He kept struggling toward the far side, the side away from his own house and nearest the Wicket Gate, and he reached it, but he could not get out because of the burden on his back. Then I saw in my dream that a man came to him whose name was Help, and asked him what he was doing there.
“Sir,” said Christian, “I was told to go this way by a man called Evangelist, who directed me to that gate over there so that I could escape the wrath to come; and as I was going, I fell in here.”
“But why didn’t you look for the steps?”
“Fear was so close behind me that I ran the nearest way, and fell in.”
“Give me your hand,” said Help. Christian gave it, and Help pulled him out and set him on solid ground and told him to go on his way. [Ps. 40:2]

Then I went up to the one who had pulled him out, and I said, “Sir, since this is the road from the City of Destruction to that gate, why isn’t this patch of ground repaired, so that poor travelers could pass more safely?”

He said to me, “This swamp is a place that cannot be repaired. It is the low ground where all the scum and filth that comes with conviction of sin keeps draining down, which is why it is called the Swamp of Despair. Whenever a sinner is awakened to his lost condition, fears and doubts and discouraging thoughts rise up in his soul, and all of them run together and settle in this place. That is why the ground here is so bad.

“It is not the King’s wish that this place should stay like this. [Isa. 35:3-4] His workmen, under the direction of His Majesty’s surveyors, have been laboring on this patch of ground for more than sixteen hundred years, trying to mend it. To my knowledge, at least twenty thousand cartloads, no, millions, of sound instructions have been swallowed up here, brought in every season from every corner of the King’s dominions; and those who know say these are the best materials there are for making good ground. But it is the Swamp of Despair still, and will be when they have done all they can.

“It is true that by the Lawgiver’s direction there are good, solid steps set right through the middle of this swamp. But at the times when the place spews up its filth the most, as it does when the weather is about to change, the steps are hard to see; or if they can be seen, men get dizzy in the head and step off them, and then they are in the mud for real, steps or no steps. But the ground is good once they are in at the gate.” [1 Sam. 12:23]

Now I saw in my dream that by this time Pliable had gotten home, and his neighbors came to visit him. Some called him a wise man for coming back; some called him a fool for risking himself with Christian; and others mocked him for his cowardice: “Well, if I had started out, I wouldn’t have been so spineless as to quit over a few difficulties.” So Pliable sat shamefaced among them. But eventually he got his confidence back, and then they all changed their tune and began to make fun of poor Christian behind his back.
And that is all there is to say about Pliable.
